name: NPO Radio 1
notes: News and sport. Lopik transmitter (the 'Gerbrandytoren', 372 m, the tallest structure in the Netherlands); other regions use other frequencies. RDS shows the station name and programme.

name: NPO Radio 2
notes: Pop music; with RDS RadioText+ the display shows artist and title. Lopik transmitter.

name: NPO 3FM
notes: Pop and alternative. Lopik transmitter.

name: NPO Klassiek
notes: Classical music: good for hearing what wideband FM stereo quality sounds like. Lopik transmitter.

name: DAB+ 12C (NPO)
notes: The NPO's DAB+ multiplex: a 1.5 MHz wide block of OFDM, a flat-topped shape in the waterfall. Use the DAB+ mode: its stations, what they play, and listen.

name: DAB+ 11C (commercial)
notes: The national commercial DAB+ multiplex (some 18 stations in one 1.5 MHz block).

name: Air guard
notes: The international aviation distress frequency: every airliner listens on it. Mostly quiet; when it isn't, something is going on (or an emergency beacon test on the hour).

name: Schiphol arrival ATIS
notes: A recorded loop with the weather, runways in use and the information letter (Alpha, Bravo…), changed every half hour. A good test signal: always on. (Frequency from public lists: check it with the Band view.)

name: Amsterdam Information
notes: Flight information for small aircraft flying under visual rules in Dutch airspace. (Frequency from public lists: check it with the Band view.)

name: Gliding
notes: A common gliding frequency in Europe: busy on sunny weekend afternoons.

name: Mil air guard
notes: The military distress frequency: exactly twice 121.5 MHz, so a transmitter on one gives a harmonic on the other.

name: ADS-B 1090
notes: Aircraft transponders, about 2 million pulses a second over the country. Use the Aircraft mode: positions, callsigns and altitudes on a map. Fact: an airliner at 11 km is heard 300+ km away.

name: ACARS 131.725
notes: Aircraft text messages (gate requests, weather, out/off/on/in times). Use the ACARS mode: it decodes 131.525, 131.725 and 131.825 at once.

name: VDL2 136.975
notes: VHF Data Link: ACARS's digital successor, over Europe busier than ACARS itself. Use the VDL2 mode: it decodes 136.725, 136.775, 136.875 and 136.975 at once, with controller-pilot messages (CPDLC). Sounds like a short hiss.

name: Shannon VOLMET
notes: Irish aviation weather for European airports, read out all day and night. Fact: a computer voice since 2005; before that, people read it live. HackRF only.

name: Shannon VOLMET 8957
notes: Aviation weather, all day. HackRF only.

name: RAF VOLMET
notes: Weather for Royal Air Force airfields. HackRF only.

name: Shanwick 8891
notes: Oceanic air traffic control for the North Atlantic (Shannon and Prestwick): aircraft without radar coverage report their position by voice. (Frequency from public lists: check it with the Band view.) HackRF only.

name: HFGCS 8992
notes: The US Air Force's worldwide HF network: now and then 'Emergency Action Messages', long strings of letters read out by an operator ('SKYKING, SKYKING, do not answer…'). Nobody outside knows what they say. HackRF only.

name: HFGCS 11175
notes: HFGCS by day: same network as 8992. HackRF only.

name: Marine ch 16
notes: Calling and distress on the water: every ship keeps a watch here. 'Mayday', 'Pan-pan' and 'Sécurité' start here.

name: Marine ch 70 DSC
notes: Digital Selective Calling: a ship's distress button sends a burst here with its position.

name: Marine ch 10
notes: Inland shipping and harbour traffic.

name: Marine ch 13
notes: Bridge to bridge: ships agreeing how to pass each other.

name: Marine ch 23 Kustwacht
notes: The Dutch Coastguard's broadcasts: weather and navigation warnings.

name: AIS 1
notes: Ships' positions. Use the Ships mode (it listens to both AIS channels at once). Fact: every ship over 300 tons must send AIS, and its range is about 40 km.

name: AIS 2
notes: The other AIS channel: ships alternate between the two.

name: 2 m FM calling
notes: Where radio amateurs call each other on 2 m FM before moving to another channel.

name: 2 m APRS
notes: Packets with positions of cars, weather stations and digipeaters. Use the APRS mode: they appear on a map. Sounds like short chirps.

name: 2 m SSB calling
notes: Long-distance 2 m contacts; in summer 'tropo' brings in stations from England and Germany.

name: 2 m FT8
notes: FT8: weak-signal data, a 15 second rhythm of tones.

name: 70 cm FM calling
notes: The 70 cm FM calling channel.

name: 70 cm SSB calling
notes: Weak-signal 70 cm.

name: 6 m FT8
notes: The 'magic band': in summer sporadic E opens it to all of Europe within minutes.

name: 6 m SSB calling
notes: 6 m SSB: quiet most of the year, crowded during openings.

name: 4 m FM calling
notes: 4 m: a band only a few European countries have.

name: 10 m FT8
notes: 10 m opens to the whole world in a solar maximum (the sun is near one now). FT8 mode.

name: 10 m FM calling
notes: FM on HF: when 10 m is open, American repeaters can be heard.

name: 23 cm SSB calling
notes: 23 cm: moon bounce stations work each other near here, bouncing signals off the moon.

name: 80 m SSB
notes: Evening and night: Dutch and Belgian amateurs talking. HackRF only.

name: 40 m SSB
notes: All of Europe by day, further at night. HackRF only.

name: 20 m FT8
notes: The busiest frequency on HF: FT8 from all over the world. Use the FT8 mode: the stations on a map. HackRF only.

name: 40 m FT8
notes: FT8 at night: all of Europe and beyond. FT8 mode. HackRF only.

name: 2 m DV calling
notes: The digital voice calling frequency on 2 m (IARU Region 1): DMR, D-STAR and YSF simplex. Use the Digital voice mode to hear the speech and who is talking.

name: 70 cm DV calling
notes: Digital voice calling on 70 cm, where most DMR simplex and hotspots are. Fact: a DMR channel carries two conversations at once, in turns of 30 milliseconds.

name: 20 m SSTV
notes: Pictures sent as sound. Use the SSTV mode (set its frequency to 14.23) to see them. HackRF only.

name: 2 m SSTV
notes: SSTV on 2 m FM (SSTV mode).

name: DAPNET pagers
notes: The radio amateurs' own pager network (POCSAG). Pick DAPNET under Settings → Modes → Pager network.

name: ISS voice and SSTV
notes: The International Space Station: crew contacts with schools, and SSTV pictures during its events. Use the Satellites mode: it follows the Doppler shift. Fact: the ISS goes round the earth every 92 minutes at 28 000 km/h.

name: ISS APRS
notes: The ISS's APRS digipeater: amateurs' packets relayed from space.

name: SO-50
notes: A small FM repeater satellite launched in 2002, still working: a few minutes of contacts per pass. Satellites mode.

name: P2000
notes: The Dutch emergency services' pager network (FLEX): every ambulance, fire and police alarm. Use the Pager mode.

name: KPN Nationaal 1
notes: Commercial POCSAG pagers (Pager mode, network KPN Nationaal 1). (Frequency from public lists: check it with the Band view.)

name: ISM 433 sensors
notes: Weather stations, thermometers, doorbells, car keys and tyre pressure sensors. Use the Sensors mode (rtl_433 knows some 250 kinds).

name: SRD 868 sensors
notes: Weather stations (Bresser and others) and smart meters (868.95 wM-Bus). Sensors mode.

name: Meshtastic
notes: Meshtastic's default LoRa channel in Europe: an off-grid text network of small radios passing messages on. LoRa chirps, 250 kHz wide; SDRadio shows them, it doesn't decode them.

name: LoRaWAN 868.1
notes: LoRa: 'chirps' sweeping up through 125 kHz, made to be heard 10+ km away with milliwatts. The Things Network's gateways listen here.

name: Sigfox 868.13
notes: Sigfox: tiny 100 Hz-wide bursts from sensors (parcel trackers, alarms).

name: PMR446 ch 1
notes: Licence-free walkie-talkies, eight channels 12.5 kHz apart (446.00625 to 446.09375). Fact: 0.5 W, but several km from a hill.

name: PMR446 ch 8
notes: PMR446 channel 8.

name: CB ch 9
notes: CB's emergency channel (AM).

name: CB ch 19
notes: Truckers' channel: in the Netherlands mostly FM.

name: C2000 TETRA
notes: The Dutch emergency services' radio network (TETRA, 390 to 395 MHz): digital and encrypted, so you only see the carriers in the waterfall.

name: Radiosondes De Bilt
notes: Weather balloons: the KNMI launches a Vaisala RS41 from De Bilt around 11:00 and 23:00 UTC; it climbs to 30+ km before the balloon bursts. Use the Radiosondes mode to follow it on a map; the frequency changes from launch to launch (400–406 MHz): sondehub.org shows the last ones.

name: Radiosondes Essen
notes: The German weather service's sondes from Essen, also an RS41; Germany launches from a dozen sites. Fact: a balloon lands up to 150 km away, and people find them.

name: DWD weather fax 3855
notes: Deutscher Wetterdienst, Pinneberg (DDH3): weather charts for ships, day and night (dial 1.9 kHz below 3855 kHz). Use the Weather fax mode. Fact: weather fax has been sent like this since the 1930s. HackRF only.

name: DWD weather fax 7880
notes: Pinneberg (DDK3) on 7880 kHz: the best by day. Surface analyses, forecasts, sea state. HackRF only.

name: DWD weather fax 13882
notes: Pinneberg (DDK6) on 13882.5 kHz. HackRF only.

name: Northwood weather fax
notes: The UK Met Office's charts from Northwood (GYA) on 4610 kHz (also 2618.5 and 8040). HackRF only.

name: Meteor-M2-3
notes: A Russian weather satellite sending pictures (LRPT). Satellites mode can record its passes for SatDump. Its frequency changes now and then.

name: Meteor-M2-4
notes: Meteor-M2-4: as M2-3. Fact: the American NOAA weather satellites that sent easy pictures on 137 MHz were switched off in 2025.

name: Iridium
notes: Satellite phones and pagers: bursts every 90 ms from 66 satellites, 780 km up. Fact: their old antennas made 'Iridium flares', flashes in the night sky.

name: Inmarsat-C
notes: Ships' safety messages from a geostationary satellite over Africa: weather, navigation warnings, distress relays. Needs a small L-band antenna. (Frequency from public lists: check it with the Band view.)

name: GPS L1
notes: GPS: you won't see it. The signal is 20 dB below the noise; receivers dig it out by correlating for a long time. Fact: each satellite sends just 50 W from 20 000 km.

name: Hydrogen line
notes: Radio astronomy: neutral hydrogen in our galaxy sends on this frequency. With a dish (or a horn) and an LNA you can map the Milky Way's arms. Protected: nothing may transmit here.

name: UVB-76 The Buzzer
notes: A Russian military station that has buzzed 25 times a minute, day and night, since the 1970s. Now and then a voice reads out names and numbers ('MDZhB…') and nobody outside knows why. Often linked to Russia's 'Dead Hand'. Parallel channel 6998 kHz. HackRF only.

name: The Buzzer 6998
notes: The Buzzer's parallel channel, since 2015. HackRF only.

name: The Pip
notes: The Buzzer's sister: short beeps, ten or so a second, now and then a voice message. 5448 kHz by day. (Not checked recently: may have moved.) HackRF only.

name: The Squeaky Wheel
notes: Another sister station: two squeaky tones repeated over and over. 3828 kHz at night. (Not checked recently: may have moved.) HackRF only.

name: Woodpecker-like OTH radar
notes: Over-the-horizon radars (Russian 'Kontayner', Chinese) still sweep the HF bands with a 'tap-tap-tap', heir to the Soviet 'Russian Woodpecker' (Duga near Chernobyl, 1976–1989). They move around: look for regular pulses between 7 and 20 MHz, in the evening. HackRF only.

name: CODAR ocean radar
notes: Coastal radars measuring sea currents send sweeping 'swoosh' chirps around 4.5–5.3, 12–13.5 and 24–27 MHz; several stand along the North Sea. HackRF only.

name: GRAVES meteor pings
notes: The French space surveillance radar near Dijon transmits continuously on 143.050 MHz. You don't hear it directly; you hear short 'pings' when a meteor's trail reflects it, dozens an hour during a shower (Perseids, Geminids). Tune 1 kHz below to hear them as tones.

name: BRAMS meteor beacon
notes: The Belgian meteor radar's beacon at Dourbes: like GRAVES, heard here only through meteor trails. Used for a citizen-science meteor count.

name: RWM time 4996
notes: Moscow's time station: second pips and a Morse ID, the Russian equivalent of DCF77. HackRF only.

name: RWM time 9996
notes: RWM by day. HackRF only.

name: WWV 10 MHz
notes: The American time station in Fort Collins, Colorado: a voice says the time every minute. Heard in Europe at night when the band is open. HackRF only.

name: CHU 7850
notes: Canada's time station: a voice in English and French and a modem burst with the time. HackRF only.

name: Channel 292
notes: A German shortwave station playing music day and night, run by enthusiasts: one of the few still on 49 m. HackRF only.

name: 13 cm SSB calling
notes: 13 cm amateur band. HackRF only.

name: Wi-Fi ch 6
notes: Wi-Fi: bursts in the waterfall (no audio). Fact: Wi-Fi shares 2.4 GHz with microwave ovens, which leak around 2450 MHz. HackRF only.

name: Microwave oven
notes: Switch on a microwave oven and watch it here: a wide, wobbling hum, 50 times a second. HackRF only.

name: Bluetooth adv 2402
notes: Bluetooth Low Energy advertising: every phone, watch and earbud blips here. HackRF only.

name: FPV R1
notes: Analog FPV drone video (Raceband R1). Use the Video mode to see the picture. HackRF only.

name: FPV F4
notes: A common FPV drone channel (Fatshark F4). Video mode. HackRF only.

name: FPV R8
notes: Raceband R8. Video mode. HackRF only.

name: 1.2 GHz video
notes: Older 1.2 GHz video senders and FPV (long range). Video mode, HackRF.

name: Russian Navy beacons 4558
notes: Single-letter Morse beacons ('C', 'D', 'P', 'S', 'M'…) of Russian naval bases, each repeating its letter day and night, a few in 100 Hz slots of one cluster. Ships and submarines use them to pick the channel that gets through. Clusters also on 3594, 5154, 7039, 8495, 10872 and 13528 kHz. HackRF only.

name: Russian Navy beacons 8495
notes: The 8 MHz cluster of the Russian Navy letter beacons: by day. HackRF only.

name: Radio Romania International
notes: Romania's international service, one of the strongest signals on shortwave in Europe, in a dozen languages; it reports on the war next door in Ukraine. Shortwave broadcasters change frequencies twice a year (March and October): check a current schedule. HackRF only.

name: Voice of Korea
notes: North Korea's state radio for the world: revolutionary songs, praise for the leader, and news from Pyongyang. Aimed at Europe in German, Russian and other languages. Also 9425 kHz. Shortwave broadcasters change frequencies twice a year (March and October): check a current schedule. HackRF only.

name: Voice of Korea 9425
notes: Voice of Korea's other frequency to Europe. Shortwave broadcasters change frequencies twice a year (March and October): check a current schedule. HackRF only.

name: China Radio International
notes: China's international radio (CRI), in German to Europe from Xi'an: China's view of the world. Shortwave broadcasters change frequencies twice a year (March and October): check a current schedule. HackRF only.

name: CRI Russian
notes: China Radio International in Russian. Shortwave broadcasters change frequencies twice a year (March and October): check a current schedule. HackRF only.

name: RRI Russian
notes: Radio Romania International in Russian: aimed at Russia, Moldova and Ukraine. Shortwave broadcasters change frequencies twice a year (March and October): check a current schedule. HackRF only.

name: HM01 Cuban numbers
notes: Cuba's numbers station: a woman reads groups of numbers, followed by digital bursts. Thought to send instructions to agents abroad. Frequencies change; Priyom.org keeps the schedules of the numbers stations still on air. (Frequency from public lists: check it with the Band view.) HackRF only.

name: NATO search and rescue
notes: The NATO and international on-scene search and rescue frequency (UHF): helicopters and lifeboats coordinate here during a rescue.

name: Military UHF air
notes: The military air band (225–400 MHz, AM): fighter jets, tankers and AWACS. Scan the band (Mil air) to find what's active near you, e.g. near Volkel or Leeuwarden air bases.

name: UHF SATCOM
notes: Military satellites in the 240–270 MHz band. Fact: the old American FLTSATCOM satellites over the Atlantic are famously hijacked by Brazilian truckers and pirates, whose voices you may hear relayed from space. (Frequency from public lists: check it with the Band view.)

name: STANAG data modem
notes: Navies send data over HF with STANAG modems: a steady warbling hiss, 2400 baud. Several sit around 4–8 MHz. (Frequency from public lists: check it with the Band view.) HackRF only.

name: ORBCOMM
notes: ORBCOMM's small data satellites (137.2–137.8 MHz): short digital bursts from trucks', ships' and pipelines' trackers. Seen with the stock antenna during a pass.

name: Meteor HRPT
notes: The Meteor satellites' high-resolution pictures (HRPT): needs a tracking dish. Fact: a 1 km resolution picture from 830 km.

name: Meteosat HRIT
notes: Meteosat, Europe's geostationary weather satellite at 36 000 km above Africa: its pictures need a 1 m dish pointed south. (Frequency from public lists: check it with the Band view.)

name: Amateur sats 145.9
notes: Several amateur satellites send their FM downlink or telemetry near 145.9 MHz; the Satellites mode follows the ISS and SO-50.
